items.title: 13.3 The bond strength of halogen molecules

source_refs.note: Topic 13.3 with Table 13.3 and the F2 drawing (printed as a second Figure 13.1), printed page 294.

blocks.text: Bond strength in the halogens decreases down the group from chlorine to iodine, because the increasing atomic size gives longer bond lengths and weaker bonds; the bond energy falls gradually from Cl2 to I2. Fluorine is the exception: its bond is relatively weak because fluorine atoms are very small, so there is significant repulsion between the lone pairs on the two atoms (Figure 13.1 shows the F2 molecule with its lone pairs), which weakens the bond despite fluorine's high electronegativity.

blocks.alt: F–F with a thick bond line. Each F atom has three orange lone-pair lobes, each holding two green dots: one above, one below and one on the outer side. Red double-headed arrows between the two upper lobes and between the two lower lobes; the label 'lp - lp repulsion' at the top.
blocks.caption: Figure 13.1: F2 molecule with lone pairs of electrons (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 13.1 on page 294; the book uses this number twice).

blocks.text: The F-F bond is weaker than the Cl-Cl bond although fluorine is the most electronegative element. Explain.
